evidence.title: Automated detection of large vessel occlusion: a multicenter study validating efficacy and proving clinical implications
evidence.outcome: Reliability of LVO probability categories versus mathematical calibration; association with infarct volume and mRS
evidence.effect: Four-category recategorization (unlikely, less likely, possible, suggestive) gave a reliable LVO estimate compared with mathematical calibration, and categories were significantly associated with follow-up infarct volume and 3-month mRS.
evidence.quote: Due to sparse data between 20-60% of LVO probabilities, recategorization into unlikely (0-20% LVO scores), less likely (20-60%), possible (60-90%), and suggestive (90-100%) provided a reliable estimation of LVO compared with mathematical calibration.

evidence.title: An Interpretable Machine Learning Tool for In-Home Screening of Agitation Episodes in People Living with Dementia
evidence.effect: Traffic-light risk stratification increased specificity by 15% and improved all metrics.
evidence.quote: Implementing the traffic-light system for risk stratification increased specificity by 15% and improved all metrics.

evidence.title: An interpretable machine learning tool for in-home monitoring of agitation episodes in people living with dementia: a proof-of-concept study
evidence.outcome: Performance of actionable traffic-light risk categories versus raw binary classification
evidence.effect: Traffic-light categories improved accuracy 71.36 to 78.87, precision 71.81 to 80.06, specificity 75.28 to 90.33, ROC AUC 77.63 to 80.73.
evidence.quote: Incorporating a stratification technique via a traffic-light system, which included an additional Amber category (medium probability estimate), increased sensitivity by 5% and specificity by 15% and improved all metrics.
evidence.sample_unit: people living with dementia (512 labelled weeks; 32,896 person-days)

commentary.bottom_line: Three offline studies, two of which appear to report the same UK dementia cohort, suggest that grouping model outputs into risk categories can keep or improve statistical performance and track outcomes. No study tested whether clinicians interpret or act on categories better than on raw probabilities, which is the hazard this recommendation targets.

perspectives.view: All three studies are offline or automated benchmarks at evidence levels 4 and 5. The two UK reports share 63 participants and 32,896 person-days, so they likely count as one dataset. The outcomes are model metrics, not clinician judgment or patient outcomes. Indirectness and imprecision support a very low certainty rating.

In the Korean stroke cohort (n=796), four large vessel occlusion categories were associated with infarct volume and 3-month mRS. This suggests the categories carry prognostic signal. No study measured missed escalations, delayed treatment, or harm from patients placed just below a cutoff, so the effect on errors reaching patients is unknown.

Traffic-light categories raised accuracy from 71.36 to 78.87 and specificity from 75.28 to 90.33 against binary classification. These gains come from how the output is thresholded, not from observed use in a workflow. No study examined alert burden, how cutoffs were set with clinicians, or whether staff followed tiered next steps.

The UK studies enrolled people living with dementia, a population of older adults with disability. No study reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. The studies also did not examine whether fixed cutoffs perform differently across subgroups.

commentary.research_gap: No study randomized or compared clinicians viewing risk categories with clinicians viewing raw probabilities to measure risk judgment, action rates, or patient outcomes. Deployers also lack tests of how cutoff placement and linked next-step pathways affect missed cases and overtreatment in live care.
commentary.underserved_note: The tests included older adults and people with disability through a UK dementia cohort. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Evidence on whether category labels help these patients and their clinicians is therefore absent, and cutoffs set in other populations may not transfer.
